concepts.topicTitle: Anatomy of the Human Eye and Function of Key Components
concepts.label: The Human Eye: Structure and How It Forms an Image
concepts.cardText: The human eye is like a camera. Its lens system forms an image on a light-sensitive screen called the retina. Light enters the eye through a thin membrane called the cornea, the transparent bulge at the front of the eyeball. Most of the refraction for the light entering the eye occurs at the outer surface of the cornea, while the crystalline lens merely provides the finer adjustment of focal length needed to focus objects at different distances on the retina. Behind the cornea is the iris, a dark muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the pupil, which regulates the amount of light entering the eye. The eye lens forms an inverted real image on the retina, whose enormous number of light-sensitive cells generate electrical signals sent to the brain by the optic nerves, and the brain interprets them so that we perceive objects as they are.

concepts.topicTitle: Power of Accommodation, Near Point and Far Point
concepts.label: Accommodation, Near Point and Far Point
concepts.cardText: The eye lens is composed of a fibrous, jelly-like material, and its curvature can be modified to some extent by the ciliary muscles, which changes its focal length. When the muscles are relaxed, the lens becomes thin and its focal length increases, so we see distant objects clearly. For nearby objects the ciliary muscles contract, increasing the curvature, so the lens becomes thicker and its focal length decreases. This ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length is called accommodation. The focal length cannot be decreased below a certain minimum, so the minimum distance at which objects can be seen distinctly without strain, the near point or least distance of distinct vision, is about 25 cm for a young adult. The far point is the farthest point the eye can see clearly, infinity for a normal eye. Cataract is the milky, cloudy crystalline lens of old age.

concepts.topicTitle: Refractive Defects of Vision and Their Correction
concepts.label: Myopia (Near-sightedness) and Its Correction
concepts.cardText: Sometimes the eye gradually loses its power of accommodation, and vision becomes blurred due to refractive defects. There are three common ones: myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia, corrected by suitable spherical lenses. Myopia, or near-sightedness, means a person sees nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly: the far point is nearer than infinity, perhaps a few metres. In a myopic eye the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina and not at the retina itself. It may arise from excessive curvature of the eye lens or elongation of the eyeball. It is corrected by a concave lens of suitable power, which brings the image back onto the retina.

concepts.topicTitle: Refractive Defects of Vision and Their Correction
concepts.label: Hypermetropia (Far-sightedness) and Its Correction
concepts.cardText: Hypermetropia, or far-sightedness, means a person can see distant objects clearly but cannot see nearby objects distinctly. The near point is farther away than the normal 25 cm, so the person has to hold reading material much beyond 25 cm for comfortable reading. This is because light rays from a closeby object are focussed at a point behind the retina. The defect arises either because the focal length of the eye lens is too long, or because the eyeball has become too small. It is corrected by a convex lens of appropriate power: eye-glasses with converging lenses provide the additional focussing power required to form the image on the retina.

concepts.topicTitle: Refractive Defects of Vision and Their Correction
concepts.label: Presbyopia and Bi-focal Lenses
concepts.cardText: The power of accommodation of the eye usually decreases with ageing, and for most people the near point gradually recedes away. They find it difficult to see nearby objects comfortably and distinctly without corrective eye-glasses; this defect is called presbyopia. It arises due to the gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens. Sometimes a person suffers from both myopia and hypermetropia and often needs bi-focal lenses, a common type having a concave upper portion that facilitates distant vision and a convex lower part that facilitates near vision. Refractive defects can also be corrected with contact lenses or surgery.

concepts.topicTitle: Refraction of Light through a Triangular Glass Prism
concepts.label: Refraction Through a Glass Prism and the Angle of Deviation
concepts.cardText: A triangular glass prism has two triangular bases and three rectangular lateral surfaces inclined to each other; the angle between its two lateral faces is the angle of the prism. In a rectangular glass slab, the parallel refracting surfaces make the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray, only displaced sideways. For a prism, the ray entering from air to glass at the first surface bends towards the normal, and at the second surface, entering from glass to air, it bends away from the normal. The peculiar shape of the prism makes the emergent ray bend at an angle to the direction of the incident ray. This angle is called the angle of deviation.

concepts.topicTitle: Dispersion of White Light, Spectrum and Rainbow Formation
concepts.label: Dispersion of White Light and the Spectrum
concepts.cardText: Sunlight passed through a narrow slit and a glass prism gives a band of colours: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red (VIBGYOR). The band of coloured components of a light beam is called its spectrum, and the splitting of light into its component colours is called dispersion. Different colours of light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through a prism: red bends the least and violet the most. So rays of each colour emerge along different paths and become distinct. Isaac Newton was the first to use a glass prism to obtain the spectrum of sunlight. He could not split the colours further with a second prism, but a second identical prism in an inverted position recombined the colours into white light, so sunlight is made up of seven colours.

concepts.topicTitle: Dispersion of White Light, Spectrum and Rainbow Formation
concepts.label: Rainbow Formation
concepts.cardText: A rainbow is a natural spectrum appearing in the sky after a rain shower. It is caused by dispersion of sunlight by tiny water droplets present in the atmosphere. A rainbow is always formed in a direction opposite to that of the Sun. The water droplets act like small prisms: they refract and disperse the incident sunlight, then reflect it internally, and finally refract it again when it comes out of the raindrop. Due to the dispersion of light and internal reflection, different colours reach the observer's eye. You can also see a rainbow on a sunny day by looking at the sky through a waterfall or water fountain with the Sun behind you.

concepts.topicTitle: Atmospheric Refraction: Star Twinkling and Advance Sunrise / Delayed Sunset
concepts.label: Twinkling of Stars and Why Planets Do Not Twinkle
concepts.cardText: Objects seen through a turbulent stream of hot air above a fire appear to waver, because hotter air is lighter and has a slightly lower refractive index than cooler air above it, and the air's conditions are not stationary. This is atmospheric refraction on a small scale. The twinkling of stars is a similar phenomenon on a larger scale. Starlight undergoes refraction continuously in the atmosphere, whose refractive index changes gradually, so it bends towards the normal and the star's apparent position differs slightly from its actual position, and keeps changing. Since stars are very distant, they approximate point-sized sources, so the amount of starlight entering the eye flickers: the star appears brighter at times and fainter at others. Planets are closer and seen as extended sources: the variations from many point-sized sources average out to zero, so they do not twinkle.

concepts.topicTitle: Atmospheric Refraction: Star Twinkling and Advance Sunrise / Delayed Sunset
concepts.label: Advance Sunrise and Delayed Sunset
concepts.cardText: Because of atmospheric refraction the Sun is visible to us about 2 minutes before the actual sunrise and about 2 minutes after the actual sunset. By actual sunrise we mean the actual crossing of the horizon by the Sun. The time difference between the actual sunset and the apparent sunset is about 2 minutes. The apparent flattening of the Sun's disc at sunrise and sunset is due to the same phenomenon.

concepts.topicTitle: Scattering of Light: Tyndall Effect, Blue Sky and Red Sunset
concepts.label: Scattering of Light and the Tyndall Effect
concepts.cardText: The earth's atmosphere is a heterogeneous mixture of minute particles such as smoke, tiny water droplets, suspended dust and air molecules. When a beam of light strikes such fine particles, its path becomes visible because the light reaches us after being reflected diffusely by the particles. This scattering of light by colloidal particles gives rise to the Tyndall effect. It is seen when a fine beam of sunlight enters a smoke-filled room through a small hole, or when sunlight passes through the mist in a dense forest. The colour of the scattered light depends on the size of the scattering particles: very fine particles scatter mainly blue light, particles of larger size scatter light of longer wavelengths, and if they are large enough the scattered light may even appear white.

concepts.topicTitle: Scattering of Light: Tyndall Effect, Blue Sky and Red Sunset
concepts.label: Why the Clear Sky Is Blue and Danger Signals Are Red
concepts.cardText: The molecules of air and other fine particles in the atmosphere have a size smaller than the wavelength of visible light. They are more effective in scattering light of shorter wavelengths at the blue end than of longer wavelengths at the red end. Red light has a wavelength about 1.8 times greater than blue light. So when sunlight passes through the atmosphere, the fine particles scatter blue (shorter wavelengths) more strongly than red, and the scattered blue light enters our eyes. If the earth had no atmosphere, there would be no scattering and the sky would look dark, as it does to passengers flying at very high altitudes. Danger signal lights are red because red is least scattered by fog or smoke, so it can be seen in the same colour at a distance.
